entries.clue: Wot! – stupid fellow getting on twice? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: TWOFOLD is used here as an adverb, 'twice over'

indicatorNotes.stupid: a stupid version of WOT is a scrambled one

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for fellow

annotation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at a dim bloke who is ageing at double speed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wot!' looks like a cry of astonishment, but it is just three letters waiting to be rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done twofold is done twice over.

entries.clue: Bollard sprayed with pee – shameful! (10)

indicatorNotes.sprayed with: spraying scatters the letters of BOLLARD and PEE together

annotation.surface: A street bollard has been used as a urinal, and a passer-by is disgusted.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's outrage is the definition itself: 'shameful!' is both the comment and the answer's meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words condemn conduct as disgraceful, and the surface's exclamation is exactly that judgement.

entries.clue: Norm vacated Conservative political group (5)

indicatorNotes.vacated: a vacated word has had its contents emptied, leaving only its outside letters

blocks.note: par = the norm, as in 'up to par'

annotation.surface: Someone called Norm has walked out of a Conservative political faction.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Norm' reads as a man's name who has quit the Tories; it is the golfing word for the standard score.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the political sense, as in the Labour Party or a party conference.

entries.clue: Brown's after bloke with topper for drink? (9)

indicatorNotes.after: TAN comes after MAN and HAT in the answer

blocks.note: a topper is a top hat

annotation.surface: Someone named Brown is chasing a man in a top hat for a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brown' is dressed as a surname with a capital letter; it is only the colour.
annotation.definitionFit: A Manhattan is a cocktail of whiskey, vermouth and bitters.

entries.clue: Tendency to breathe fast embracing topless old-fashioned girl (8)

indicatorNotes.embracing: PANT holds the other piece in its arms

blocks.note: to pant is to breathe fast
WENCH, an old word for a girl, without its first letter

annotation.surface: A leering man pants over a topless girl, and it is framed as his bent.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'old-fashioned girl' is a wench, a word now only found in historical fiction.
annotation.definitionFit: A penchant is a liking or tendency towards something.

entries.clue: Private Eye is going to source (4)

blocks.note: a magazine speaks of itself as 'we'

annotation.surface: The magazine announces that it is about to go to a source for a story.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is printed in Private Eye, so 'Private Eye is going to' is the magazine saying WE'LL; 'source' is then read as a spring rather than an informant.
annotation.definitionFit: A well is a source of water, and figuratively of anything.

entries.clue: Join together to secure Rishi's end – and flourish (5)

indicatorNotes.to secure: WELD holds the letter fast inside it
indicatorNotes.end: only the final letter of Rishi is used

blocks.note: to weld is to join metal together

annotation.surface: A political alliance forms to finish off Rishi Sunak, and then thrives.
annotation.walkthrough: Rishi is Rishi Sunak, the former Conservative prime minister; the clue only needs his final letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Flourish as a verb means to brandish, and brandishing a weapon is handling it with display.

entries.clue: Finished importing Republicans new weapon? (5)

indicatorNotes.importing: DONE brings the letter in from outside

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

annotation.surface: Having finished, the Republicans bring in some novel armament.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as loose: a drone is a relatively recent weapon, not the only one.
annotation.definitionFit: Armed drones are a modern addition to warfare.

entries.clue: see 26dn. (9)
"Patel not finished infiltrating South East" – Gnome (6)

indicatorNotes.not finished: PRITI stops short of its last letter
indicatorNotes.infiltrating: the shortened name gets inside SE

blocks.note: PRITI Patel without her last letter
S and E, the compass-point abbreviations for south and east

annotation.surface: The satirical Gnome, Private Eye's mock proprietor, reports Priti Patel seeping into the South East.
annotation.walkthrough: Priti Patel is a Conservative politician and former Home Secretary; Lord Gnome is Private Eye's fictional owner, so the quotation looks like his byline.
annotation.definitionFit: A sprite is a fairy or elf, the same order of small creature as a gnome.

entries.clue: Unpleasant consequences of trip published (7)

blocks.note: a book that is published is out

annotation.surface: A trip abroad has been made public, and there are awkward repercussions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trip' suggests a journey, perhaps a junket that leaked; it is a stumble.
annotation.definitionFit: Originally radioactive dust after a nuclear blast; figuratively, the damaging after-effects of any event.

entries.clue: Blimey, Latin TV series, one to annoy a politician? (7)

blocks.note: heck! and blimey! are both mild exclamations

annotation.surface: Someone exclaims at a Latin television show and wonders who might irritate an MP.
annotation.walkthrough: Blimey is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'heck'. The question mark flags a definition by example: hecklers annoy anyone on stage.
annotation.definitionFit: A heckler interrupts a speaker, classically a politician at a hustings.

entries.clue: Large, more erect – not the first to show reserve (6)

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: Something big and increasingly upright is not the first to hold back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' reads as a verb or as shyness; here it is a noun, a store of food.
annotation.definitionFit: A larder is where a household keeps its reserve of food.

entries.clue: Blunt? Yes and no (8)

blocks.note: reads as the adjective frank, but the capital and question mark also point to the spy Anthony Blunt
the answer fits the ordinary adjective but not the man

annotation.walkthrough: Anthony Blunt was the art historian exposed as a Soviet spy, and he was gay: so STRAIGHT means blunt (yes), but Blunt was neither honest nor heterosexual (no).
annotation.definitionFit: Straight talk is blunt, frank talk.

entries.clue: Large newspaper comes up with raving nut again (not Independent) (10)

indicatorNotes.comes up: in a down entry, RAG read upwards
indicatorNotes.not Independent: the I for Independent is taken out

blocks.note: a rag is a disreputable newspaper, reversed
anagram fodder: NUT plus AGAIN minus I

annotation.surface: A big newspaper runs another story on a raving crank, but the Independent stays out of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Large newspaper' wants to be a broadsheet; Large is the definition and the paper is a rag. I = Independent is a standard abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Gargantuan means enormous, after Rabelais's giant Gargantua.

entries.clue: Rival has a date with king since rising in mighty surroundings (9)

indicatorNotes.rising: in a down entry, AS goes upwards to SA
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places R and SA within VERY, the way an object sits inside a container

blocks.note: as = since, as in 'as it's late'

annotation.surface: A rival has a date with a king ever since coming up in powerful circles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mighty' sounds like a noun for the powerful; it is the informal adverb meaning very.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an opponent in a contest or conflict.

entries.clue: Vulgar tosser, Clarkson? (11)

blocks.note: one who casts is one who tosses

annotation.surface: An insult hurled at Jeremy Clarkson, the loud-mouthed motoring presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tosser' is British slang for a contemptible man, which is how the surface reads it; here it is literally one who tosses. The question mark marks Clarkson as one example of a broadcaster.
annotation.definitionFit: Jeremy Clarkson, of Top Gear, is a television broadcaster.

entries.clue: Making a broadcast? Note: hair needs curling (2,3,3)

indicatorNotes.curling: curled letters are twisted into a new order

annotation.surface: A memo reminds a presenter to curl their hair before going live.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface follows on from 17 across, a presenter preparing for camera.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a presenter who is live is said to be on the air; the question mark allows the phrase for the act.

entries.clue: Boris trashed in a book – Cyclops goes "Suck it up!" (6)

indicatorNotes.trashed: trashing BORS wrecks its letter order
indicatorNotes.in: the jumble sits inside A and B

blocks.note: a + B, the abbreviation for book
the setter Cyclops refers to himself as I; that I is removed from BORIS

annotation.surface: Boris Johnson is savaged in a book, and the setter tells him to take it.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself means I. 'Suck it up!' as an order to endure criticism is the surface; as a literal instruction it means absorb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both literal (a sponge soaking up water) and figurative (taking criticism without complaint).

entries.clue: Teach Conservative candidate finally to embrace old money (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: take the final letters of Conservative and candidate
indicatorNotes.to embrace: the two Es hold the coin between them

blocks.note: last letters of Conservative and candidate
the ducat, an old European gold coin

annotation.surface: A Tory hopeful is urged to court old-money donors to learn the ropes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old money' suggests the landed gentry; here it is a historical coin.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to instruct someone, whether in school or in life.

entries.clue: Rest about to get stuck into 'dippy' type (8)

blocks.note: a bather is one who takes a dip

annotation.surface: Someone takes a break before tackling a scatterbrained sort.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'dippy' hint that it is not 'silly' but 'given to dipping': a swimmer.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a pause long enough to catch one's breath.

entries.clue: Sheeran has series of battles with duke, a major royal (6)

blocks.note: a war is a series of battles

annotation.surface: Ed Sheeran is feuding with a duke and a senior royal.
annotation.walkthrough: The name has been borne by many kings of England and by Prince Edward, the Duke of Edinburgh.

entries.clue: What did Fujitsu/Horizon fail to do properly? Budge, stupid! (5)

annotation.definition: What did Fujitsu/Horizon fail to do properly?

indicatorNotes.stupid: a stupid BUDGE has its letters in a daft order

annotation.surface: An exasperated question about the Post Office Horizon scandal, then an order to shift.
annotation.walkthrough: Horizon was the faulty Fujitsu accounting software behind the Post Office scandal, in which hundreds of British sub-postmasters were wrongly prosecuted.

entries.clue: Good TV personality – or offensive? (5)

blocks.note: Jonathan Ross, the British chat-show host

annotation.surface: Is a certain TV presenter a nice guy, or objectionable?
annotation.walkthrough: Jonathan Ross is a British television presenter who once caused a scandal over offensive prank calls, which gives the question an edge.
annotation.definitionFit: Gross behaviour is offensive, disgusting behaviour.

entries.clue: Rest arranged after lads head off for aphrodisiacs (7)

indicatorNotes.after: the jumble comes after the shortened lads

entries.clue: (& 9ac.) Quality not possessed by Liz Truss? 'Putting out feelers' was ans. (4)

annotation.definition: Quality not possessed by Liz Truss?

indicatorNotes.Putting out: to put out is to disturb, so the letters are thrown into disorder

entries.clue: Nick, old jerk relying on AI (7)

blocks.note: to nick is British slang for to steal, to rob

entries.clue: Abuse of one's public position is hard work! (5)
